title: Tale of the First Attendant Bukhayt

keywords: tale of the first eunuch bukhayt
full_text:
While the three slaves were carrying the chest containing Kutan-al-Qulub to the cemetery, they sat upon a tombstone to rest, and the first attendant, Bukhayt, explained how he had entered royal service:

"In my youth, I was a farm hand in Upper Egypt, but I possessed a mischievous disposition that took delight in sowing mischief between peaceful neighbors. If I saw two farmers working harmoniously, I would whisper to the first that his companion was stealing his irrigation water, and whisper to the second that his neighbor had cursed his oxen.

One day, my master, an honest cattle breeder, purchased a spirited bull. Desiring to test my cunning, I whispered to the master’s wife that her husband intended to sell her bridal jewelry, and told the master that his wife had consulted an astrologer to leave him. Both flew into a furious temper, shouting accusations across the courtyard.

In the confusion of their quarrel, the farm gate was left unlatched. The spirited bull charged out into the vegetable gardens, knocked over the beehives, and trampled the master’s prize melons. The furious bees swarmed upon the household, stinging the master, his wife, and myself until we looked like spotted leopards!

When the uproar subsided and the master discovered that my deceitful whispers had orchestrated the entire catastrophe, he seized an ox-whip and gave me a hundred lashes. He shaved my head, branded my forehead with the mark of a slanderer, and sold me to a foreign caravan driver for three silver coins. That painful day taught me that he who lights the fire of malice in another’s home will find his own beard singed by the flames."
moral: Sowing discord between others creates a fire that eventually consumes the troublemaker himself.
